thesisQuality.basis: Essential regulated grid assets and visible rate-base investment support durable value capture.

financialOperatingMomentum.basis: Profitable operations and raised guidance tempered by capital needs.

catalystScore.basis: Large-load commitments, approvals and rate-base deployment provide catalysts.

governancePower.basis: Capital allocation disciplined by commissions and guidance.

alignment2036.basis: Grid infrastructure is foundational for electrification, industry and compute demand.

crossDivisionLeverage.basis: Generation, transmission and distribution serve multiple customer classes.

bottleneckControl.basis: AEP controls regulated grid and interconnection pathways where capacity is constrained.

supplyChainResilience.basis: Scale helps planning but equipment and permitting bottlenecks remain.

dataConfidenceEvidence.basis: Current SEC/issuer financial and load evidence plus market context cover required factors; customer-level firmness remains partly undisclosed.

scoreRecord.thesis: AEP controls essential regulated grid infrastructure in territories seeing strong load growth, creating long-duration rate-base growth if demand converts and recovery is timely.
scoreRecord.keyRisk: Capital can be deployed ahead of realized load or at unfavorable financing cost while regulatory constraints delay recovery.
scoreRecord.nextCatalyst: Further conversion of large-load commitments into approved projects and updated earnings/capital guidance.

items.risk: Converting prospective load into earnings requires generation/transmission buildout, regulatory approvals, customer commitments and capital execution.
Massive load/capex opportunity can pressure affordability and financing if demand timing or regulatory recovery lags investment.
Generation availability, turbine supply, permitting and regulatory approvals can become successor bottlenecks after transmission demand is identified.
Capital intensity requires substantial debt/equity financing; higher funding costs or weaker credit metrics can erode shareholder economics.
Large-load contracts still require generation, transmission, permits and regulatory cost recovery; signed demand is not equivalent to realized energized load.
Affordability pressure can constrain rate recovery even when infrastructure need is genuine.
